scenes.visual: Title card: When Experience Arrives. Subtitle: Song, sight and language. Replace the door-and-tide framing.

scenes.tts: A young male white-crowned sparrow never hears an adult sing. As an adult, its song is simple and abnormal. Hearing the right song later does little to fix it. The same experience can have a lasting effect at one age and little effect at another. Genes and experience shape when learning can happen. Experience can even help close the window. Timing matters because missing early input can leave lasting deficits in song and sight, and late language access affects later proficiency.

scenes.visual: Show a sparrow raised without adult song, its simple adult song beside a detailed wild song, and late tutoring with little change. Then compare the same input arriving at different developmental ages and producing different lasting outcomes. Show genes and prior experience feeding into a learning window; label the main question: When does input arrive, and what lasts?

scenes.tts: Genes build the circuit that can learn and set roughly when it can learn. Experience supplies what is learned. In zebra finches, birds raised without a tutor can still copy new song after birds raised with a tutor have stopped. That suggests hearing a tutor helps close the window. Age alone does not set it.

scenes.visual: Replace the door/tide definitions with a comparison of zebra finches raised with and without a tutor. At the same later age, introduce a new tutor: the previously isolated bird copies it while the normally reared bird does not. Use schematic timelines without numerical ages. Link genes to the learning circuit and prior tutoring to window closure.

scenes.tts: What happens inside that window? Song learning has two phases. A young bird listens to a tutor and memorizes the song. Then it practices, shaping its own sounds to match the memory. In white-crowned sparrows, these phases can be months apart. A sparrow deafened between them sings a very poor song. It must hear itself to correct its voice. The brain has a motor pathway from H V C through R A to the brainstem. Another pathway, through area X and L man, matters while song is learned.

scenes.visual: Show listening depositing a tutor-song memory, then practice and an auditory feedback loop comparing the bird’s voice with that memory. Show deafening between phases disrupting the adult song. Add a compact circuit diagram: HVC to RA to brainstem to syrinx; a second route from HVC through area X, thalamus and LMAN back to RA, labelled learning. Keep the thalamus in the diagram even though the narration abbreviates the route.

scenes.tts: Sight has different windows for different abilities. Infants born with dense cataracts show what visual input does. Right after treatment, infants' acuity was no better than a newborn's, whatever their age. Some improvement appeared after as little as an hour of visual input. Patterned input drives improvement. Yet fine acuity and processing the spacing of facial features showed lasting deficits after early deprivation. Early input can matter even before an ability appears. Improvement and lasting loss can coexist.

scenes.visual: Move this scene before language. Show a cloudy lens admitting diffuse light, then treatment admitting patterned input. Plot acuity starting at the newborn level and improving after input, with no invented numerical scale. Show separate tracks for fine acuity and facial-feature spacing retaining deficits. End with distinct function-specific windows and an early-input band preceding a later-emerging ability. Remove sample-size dots and the preferential-looking demonstration.

scenes.tts: For language, ask first about access to a first language. Some deaf children of hearing parents first meet a signed language late. Delayed access affects later proficiency. These children mainly lacked an accessible language, rather than the whole range of care and social contact.

scenes.visual: Add a scene before the second-language comparison. Show early versus delayed access to a signed first language, with later proficiency as the outcome. Keep care and social contact visible in both tracks so the animation does not imply general social isolation. Do not draw a universal cutoff or a numerical score.

scenes.tts: Learning a second language asks a different question. These learners already know a first language. Researchers compared English grammar scores with age of arrival. The youngest arrivals scored like native speakers. Scores fell with age up to about puberty. Later arrivals scored lower and varied widely. The age effect is clear. Its cause remains debated: changes in plasticity, an established first language, or differences in input.

Show grammar scores against age of arrival: native-like for the youngest, declining up to about puberty, then lower and scattered. Use qualitative axes without invented values or a universal cutoff. scenes.tts: Across these cases, ask what input arrives, at what age, and what lasts. Experience shapes learning, and can help shape the window itself.

End card echoing the new title, When Experience Arrives, with song, sight and language icons. No door/tide rule.
